meta.title: Who really said "In essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Augustine. The maxim's earliest known source is Marco Antonio de Dominis's De republica ecclesiastica (1617). Rupertus Meldenius used it in 1626 and long got the credit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Augustine. It is first found in de Dominis's 1617 De republica ecclesiastica and was long credited to Rupertus Meldenius (1626).

answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — earliest known in Marco Antonio de Dominis
answer.sourceLine: No one has located this maxim in Augustine’s writings. Its earliest known form is Latin, in de Dominis’s De republica ecclesiastica (London, 1617): “unitatem in necessariis, in non necessariis libertatem, in omnibus caritatem.” The Lutheran Rupertus Meldenius (Peter Meiderlin) used it in 1626 and long got the credit for it.

source.heading: Where the maxim actually first appears

docMeta.dd: Latin. The popular English wording is an anonymous rendering.

source.excerpt: Omnesque mutuam amplecteremur unitatem in necessariis, in non necessariis libertatem, in omnibus caritatem.
trail: Wikiquote lists the maxim in the Misattributed section of its Augustine page. It gives the “first known occurrence” as de Dominis, De Republica Ecclesiastica, London (1617), lib. 4 cap. 8, p. 676 (Wikiquote ↗).

The Augustine scholar James J. O’Donnell could not find the saying in Augustine’s writings. His page also reproduces Steve Perisho’s summary of H. J. M. Nellen (1999), which traces the earlier de Dominis form, where scholars had previously credited Peter Meiderlin, alias Meldenius (Georgetown ↗; Perisho ↗).
The Schaff-Herzog encyclopedia identifies “Rupertus Meldenius” as the pseudonym of Peter Meiderlin. It dates his Paraenesis votiva pro pace ecclesiae to Rottenburg, 1626 (CCEL ↗).
In 1959 Pope John XXIII quoted it only as “the common saying, expressed in various ways and attributed to various authors” (Ad Petri cathedram, §72, Vatican ↗).
source.excerptNote: Our literal gloss: “And let us all mutually embrace unity in necessary things, liberty in non-necessary things, charity in all things.” The Latin is as reproduced on Wikiquote ↗ and Wikipedia ↗. Meldenius’s 1626 version ends “in utrisque” (“in both”) rather than “in omnibus” (“in all things”).

source.rightsNote: The Latin source, de Dominis’s De republica ecclesiastica (London, 1617), has long been in the public domain. The English wording people quote, “In essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity,” is an anonymous rendering with no identifiable translator or first printing, so we make no rights claim about it.
source.useLine: The Latin original (1617) is long public domain; the popular English wording has no identifiable translator or first printing, so we give no rights status for it.

author.name: Marco Antonio de Dominis
author.heading: About the true source
author.bio: Born on the island of Rab in 1560, de Dominis became Archbishop of Split in 1602. Fearing the Inquisition, he left for England in 1616, where the first part of his anti-papal De republica ecclesiastica appeared in London in 1617. He later returned to Rome, died in September 1624 while confined in Castel Sant’Angelo, and was condemned as a relapsed heretic after his death; his body and works were burned on 21 December 1624.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: The maxim is pinned on Augustine far more often than on anyone else. For more than a century scholars credited a minor Lutheran pamphleteer instead, until an earlier source turned up in 1999.

items.why: O’Donnell could not find it in Augustine’s writings and notes that Schaff’s History of the Christian Church calls the Augustine attribution false (Georgetown ↗). Wikiquote files it under Misattributed (Wikiquote ↗). Catholic Answers says no one has identified where in his works it would appear (Catholic Answers ↗).

His irenic tract Paraenesis votiva pro pace ecclesiae, published under the pseudonym Rupertus Meldenius (Rottenburg, 1626; Schaff-Herzog ↗), puts it as a wish: “Si nos servaremus in necessariis Unitatem, in non-necessariis Libertatem, in utrisque Charitatem” (Wikipedia ↗). Some sources date the tract to about 1627 (Ligonier ↗). Nellen’s 1999 article showed that de Dominis had already used the phrase, overturning the older consensus (Wikipedia ↗).

Schaff’s note, quoted on O’Donnell’s page, says Gregor Frank used the phrase in 1628, and that Conrad Bergius passed it on, crediting Meldenius, to Richard Baxter, who repeated it in 1680 as “that of Rupertus Meldenius, cited by Conradus Bergius” (Georgetown ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest known occurrence is Marco Antonio de Dominis, De republica ecclesiastica, vol. 1 (London, 1617), book 4, chapter 8, p. 676, in Latin (Wikiquote ↗; Perisho on Nellen ↗).

context.heading: A peace formula for divided churches
lead: The maxim was coined as a plea for Christian peace, not as patristic wisdom. De Dominis wrote it in an anti-papal treatise published in London. Meldenius, a Lutheran writing “at the time of the Thirty Years’ War,” used it to urge his fellow Augsburg Confession theologians toward concord (Schaff-Herzog ↗). Its “necessary” things were the doctrines needed for salvation.

Later, mostly Catholic, users swapped non necessariis (“non-essentials”) for dubiis (“doubtful things”). The historian Joseph Lecler argued that the change stretched liberty to every undefined question (Wikipedia ↗). That “doubtful matters” form is the one John XXIII quoted in 1959. The popular English “non-essentials … all things” follows de Dominis’s own pattern, in non necessariis … in omnibus.
context.detailsSummary: Why does Augustine get the credit?
detailsBody: Nobody has documented how the maxim came to be pinned on Augustine. A likely reason, offered here as our inference, is that a short, balanced Latin line about unity and charity sounds like a Church Father, and Augustine is the Latin Father whose name most readily attracts such sayings. Even the Vatican in 1959 declined to name an author (Ad Petri cathedram §72 ↗).
context.pull: “The common saying, expressed in various ways and attributed to various authors.” — John XXIII, 1959

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Augustine page lists 'In necessariis unitas, in dubiis libertas, in omnibus caritas' under its Misattributed heading and gives the first known occurrence as de Dominis, De Republica Ecclesiastica, Pars I, London (1617), lib. 4 cap. 8, p. 676

Wikipedia: the maxim is often misattributed to Augustine; it seems first used in 1617 by de Dominis (De Republica Ecclesiastica, bk 4 ch 8, p. 676), with the Latin passage; consensus formerly credited Meiderlin/Meldenius (Paraenesis votiva, 1626, 'in utrisque Charitatem'); Nellen 1999 overturned that; Lecler on the 'dubiis' substitution

O'Donnell could not find the saying in Augustine; Schaff calls the Augustine attribution false; Meldenius was the usual credit; Gregor Frank, Conrad Bergius and Richard Baxter also used it; Nellen (1999) found the earlier de Dominis form (London, 1617)

Ad Petri cathedram §72 (29 June 1959): 'But the common saying, expressed in various ways and attributed to various authors, must be recalled with approval: in essentials, unity; in doubtful matters, liberty; in all things, charity.'

Schaff-Herzog: Rupertus Meldenius is the pseudonym of Peter Meiderlin, a German Lutheran theologian writing at the time of the Thirty Years' War; Paraenesis votiva pro pace ecclesiae, Rottenburg, 1626; motto 'in necessariis ... in non necessariis libertas, in utrisque caritas'

Perisho: the earliest known occurrence is de Dominis, De republica ecclesiastica, vol. 1, bk 4 ch 8, p. 676 (London, 1617), 'vnitatem in necessarijs, in non necessarijs libertatem, in omnibus caritatem'; Nellen 1999; Lecler on the dubiis variant
Catholic Answers: the saying is usually attributed to Augustine, but no one has identified where in his works it appears
Ligonier: often attributed to Augustine, the saying comes from Rupertus Meldenius, in a tract written circa 1627

de Dominis was born on Rab in 1560, became Archbishop of Split in 1602, left for England in 1616, published De republica ecclesiastica vol. 1 in London in 1617, died in September 1624 confined in Castel Sant'Angelo, and his body and works were burned on 21 December 1624
